C4b.object: a signed, encrypted proof-of-learning (training record) timestamped or published to a public ledger after training, to defeat replay/first-publication disputes; not a preregistration, not anchored before data, stranger re-verification not specified
C4b.quote: The proof (or its signature) can be timestamped, or published in a public ledger. This ensures that verifying its validity is as simple as a lookup operation. This prevents replay attacks
C4b.reason: Public-ledger anchoring of a hash/signature is the same mechanism, but the anchored object is a post-hoc training proof rather than a frozen preregistration before any data, so OCCUPIES.

pass1.object: a proof of training, or its signature, published to a public ledger
pass1.quote: The proof (or its signature) can be timestamped, or published in a public ledger.

bearing_quotes: When developing our concept for PoL, we consider only the training phase and not the inference phase; the cost of inference is generally much lower, and there already exist mechanisms to ensure the integrity of ML inference performed by another party [14].

The proof (or its signature) can be timestamped, or published in a public ledger. This ensures that verifying its validity is as simple as a lookup operation. This prevents replay attacks, where A would claim to have published the PoL first.
if the trainer produces a PoL and publishes a time-stamped signature of it, this unchangeable record proves ownership in case of false claim by a surrogate model owner.
We tolerate d2(W′t+k,W t+k) ≤ δ, where d2 is a distance measure (possibly different from d1). δ is a slack parameter that should be calibrated before verification starts
Since the purpose of δ is to upper bound the randomness in training, one heuristic is to set δ as the average of a few gradient updates during training.
Alternatively, acceptable ranges for δ may be mandated by law and enforced by the verifier.
where zt is the random variable representing noise arising from the hardware and low-level libraries such as cuDNN [73] at step t
we require that maxt εrepr(t) ≪ dref, where dref = d(W1T, W2T) is the reference distance between two models W1T and W2T of the same architecture, trained to completion
then we can set our distance threshold δ (refer to Algorithm 2) such that maxt(εrepr(t)) < δ < dref.

Note that this error accumulates even when using the exact same batching strategy, architecture, initial parameters, and training setup, due to the irreproducible noise z arising from the hardware and low-level libraries.
||εrepr|| with deterministic operations drops to half of ||εrepr|| for non-deterministic operations with ResNet-20. However, ||εrepr|| is still significant
Theorem 1 also proves that the exact reproducibility of a ML model is difficult because the entropy grows, without bound, as the training sequence grows
verification should succeed even if the verifier uses different hardware than the prover.
counter-based pseudorandom number generators [86], [87] can potentially remove most, if not all, noise in the training process
follow up work may consider hashing weights sequentially utilizing Merkle tree structure [85], i.e. each consecutive set of weights during the training procedure are hashed
The verifier keeps a record of previously verified proofs. Therefore, in Algorithm 2, if V has recorded P 0, VERIFY INIT PROOF would be a simple record lookup.
our probability of success for our verification scheme degrades multiplicatively with each usage.

[S13 full read] Table 2 (§2.4) is a rejected logit-similarity baseline: JSD of logits on a single fixed string, cited to Chen et al. 2022a 'Copy, right?' (IEEE S&P 2022) — that cited work may bear on C4a more directly than S13 does.
[S13 full read] The MD5 variant hashes the secret key, not the probe set; no hashed item set anywhere in the paper.

[S13 full read] Table 5 p-values are one-sample t-tests against a fixed 75% threshold over 10 sampled reruns of the derivative model — a repeated-run measure, but not a same-weights floor for a comparison.

[S14 full read] Yang & Wu 2024, 'A fingerprint for large language models' (arXiv:2407.01235) — the 'Logits method' baseline compares output-logit spaces of victim and suspect; closer to C4a's log-probability object than REEF itself and should be surveyed.

[S14 full read] Iourovitski et al. 2024 (arXiv:2408.02871) and Pasquini et al. 2024 LLMmap (arXiv:2407.15847) are cited as black-box behavioural fingerprints from generated content — possible C4a neighbours.
[S14 full read] Table 1 reports the Logits method giving 0.9999 on many derivatives and 0.0000 under permutation with no interval, i.e. point similarities only.

[S17 full read] Stage 3 of §3.4 (identical hardware, updated stack, consecutive reruns) is the closest published analogue to an in-situ same-weights floor; it is used to caveat method comparisons, not to fingerprint a served model.

[S17 full read] Atil et al. 2025, 'Non-determinism of "deterministic" llm settings' (arXiv:2408.04667) and He & Thinking Machines 2025 'Defeating nondeterminism in llm inference' are cited for the floor's cause — both may bear on C4a's same-weights floor and should be surveyed.

[S17 full read] Madaan et al. 2024 'Quantifying variance in evaluation benchmarks' (arXiv:2406.10229) and Bowyer et al. 2025 'Don't use the CLT in LLM evals with fewer than a few hundred datapoints' (arXiv:2503.01747) are cited for interval methodology on small item sets.
[S17 full read] All measurements are sampling-based (temperature 0.8, top_p 0.9); the paper never uses teacher-forced log-probabilities.
